claims.text: Enhanced anchoring increases the thermal stability of multi-element, near-equiatomic nanoparticles.
Enhanced anchoring increases the chemical stability of multi-element, near-equiatomic nanoparticles.
Graphene functionalization reduces nanoparticle sintering at high temperature.
Graphene functionalization reduces phase degradation at high temperature.
The initial nanoparticles have a uniform elemental distribution.
A graphene layer on the support strengthens nanoparticle–support interfacial bonding.
Stronger nanoparticle–support interfacial bonding limits atomic diffusion.
Stronger nanoparticle–support interfacial bonding restricts nanoparticle agglomeration.
Stronger nanoparticle–support interfacial bonding restricts phase separation.
Limiting diffusion, agglomeration, and phase separation preserves nanoparticle structure and chemical uniformity under thermal stress.
Graphene-functionalized samples will show less sintering than samples on unfunctionalized supports under otherwise identical high-temperature conditions.
Graphene-functionalized samples will show less phase degradation than samples on unfunctionalized supports under otherwise identical high-temperature conditions.
Graphene-functionalized samples will retain chemical stability better than samples on unfunctionalized supports under otherwise identical high-temperature conditions.
The proposed stabilization mechanism is expected to apply when oxidation and support degradation are minimal.
The proposed stabilization mechanism may fail in strongly oxidative environments.
